archetype.name: Bubble Team (goalie-first)
archetype.definition: A team that loses the shot and chance battle most nights and stays in the playoff conversation because its goaltending and penalty kill erase the gap, which leaves little margin when the saves dip.

report.headline: Sorokin and the PK are holding up a team that gets outshot nightly
report.take:
The Islanders are 9-6-4 with 22 standings points. That is a 95-point pace, ahead of last season's 91. On the site they sit 16th of 32, which is about right: a bubble team in a Metropolitan Division where Carolina and New Jersey have already pulled away. They score at a league-average rate (3.16 a game against a league mark of 3.17) and allow fewer than most (2.95, 12th). Read only the scoreboard and they look like a sound, slightly above-average club.

The process numbers tell a different story. New York takes 25.5 shots a game (27th) and allows 28.8 (26th). At 5-on-5 it owns 48.7% of the expected goals (20th) and 48% of the shot attempts (22nd). The gap closes in two places. The first is the goalies: they are 11.9 goals saved above expected, third in the league, with a combined .911 save percentage that also ranks third. The second is a penalty kill at 85.9%, fourth in the league. The forwards have also finished well, with a 12.2% shooting rate (9th). Simon Holmstrom has 9 goals on 35 shots and Victor Eklund 7 on 29. Put together, that is an all-situations PDO of 103.2, fourth highest, and a 5-on-5 PDO of 102.3. The Pts vs Goal Diff mark is -0.4, so the standings are not inflated by overtime luck. The goal differential itself is the part propped up by percentages.

History says this is not a fluke so much as an identity. Last season they finished with a 0.48 xGF%, a 5th-ranked defense and 40.1 goals saved above expected. In 2022-23 the goalie figure was 41.1. Elite goaltending is the one thing this franchise has repeatedly sustained. Ilya Sorokin (.915, 8.5 GSAx, 9th of 71 goalies) is the main reason. Semyon Varlamov has posted 5.2 GSAx in six starts despite an .899 save percentage, which says he has been facing dangerous shots. The skaters lean hard on two players. Matthew Schaefer is 5th of 259 defensemen, playing almost 27 minutes with 21 points, and Bo Horvat has 20 points with 7 on the power play. Behind Schaefer the blueline grades a D. Adam Pelech (0.416 xGF%), Ryan Pulock (0.42) and Tony DeAngelo (-9) are losing their minutes. The power play converts just 17.2% (28th), the same weakness it was last year.

The recent trend is mixed. Over the last 10 games they went 4-3-3 and allowed 3.6 goals a game, 0.65 more than their season rate. Three one-goal overtime losses in that run turned possible wins into single points. The last two games were convincing road wins: 5-2 at Los Angeles and 6-2 at Anaheim. Expect the shooting percentage to cool. Expect the goaltending to stay good, though probably not third-in-the-league good. That points to a team hovering around a wild-card line rather than pulling away from it.

strengths.title: Goaltending that steals games
strengths.body: The goalies have saved 11.9 goals above expected, third in the league, and that is the main reason a team that gets outshot allows fewer goals than most. Sorokin carries the load, and Varlamov's positive GSAx in his starts means there is no drop-off on back-to-backs. Last season's 40.1 GSAx shows this is a repeatable strength rather than a hot month, though the current rate will likely ease somewhat.

strengths.title: A top-five penalty kill
strengths.body: The kill runs at 85.9%, fourth in the league and well above the league average of 77.4%. Strong goaltending fuels it, since the kill is where goalies face the most dangerous shots. Kills built on save percentage wobble more than ones built on suppression, but with this tandem it should stay above average.

strengths.title: Schaefer driving the blueline
strengths.body: Matthew Schaefer is the 5th-ranked defenseman on the site. He plays 26.97 minutes a night and has 21 points, more than any forward, with 7 on the power play. He is the only defenseman here who drives offense, which makes him invaluable and also explains why the group grade collapses behind him.

concerns.title: Outshot and out-chanced at 5-on-5
concerns.body: New York ranks 27th in shots for and 26th in shots against, with a 48.7% expected-goals share. The goal differential is positive only because the team is fourth in all-situations PDO at 103.2. Shooting at 12.2% is the piece most likely to fade. When it does, the margin shrinks toward even unless the shot share improves.

concerns.title: A power play that doesn't threaten
concerns.body: At 17.2% the power play ranks 28th, five points below the league average. It is a multi-year problem: 16.5% last season and 12.6% the year before. With so few shots at even strength, the team badly needs the man advantage to produce, and Horvat and Schaefer are doing most of the work there.

concerns.title: Thin defense behind Schaefer, leaking lately
concerns.body: The blueline grades a D. Pelech (0.416 xGF%) and Pulock (0.42) are being badly out-chanced in heavy minutes. Goals against have climbed to 3.6 a game over the last 10, up 0.65 from the season rate. If the goalies cool while this persists, the defensive ranking will slide.

trend.note: They hovered around .500 in decisions through October and have banked loser points in November. The last 10 went 4-3-3 with more goals against than usual, but two lopsided wins to close the trip suggest the offense is warming.

weekAhead.headline: Four games against teams ranked below them, three with leaky penalty kills
weekAhead.body:
All four opponents sit below New York on the site. Columbus (27th) scores at the league's lowest shooting percentage. Winnipeg allows the most shots in the league and has a .881 team save percentage. Detroit ranks 27th in offense. Toronto is 25th with a 46.1% expected-goals share. None of these teams is likely to exploit the Islanders' shot deficit the way Carolina or Edmonton did.

The road games in Winnipeg and Detroit are the swing. Both teams kill penalties poorly, 72.1% and 71.4%, which gives the struggling power play its best opening in a while. Toronto's 6th-ranked power play against the 4th-ranked Islanders kill is the toughest special-teams matchup of the week. Three or more wins is a reasonable expectation.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against Winnipeg
keyMatchups.body: The Jets allow 32 shots a game, last in the league, and give up the most points to defensemen relative to expectation (29th). That suits a team that usually struggles to get pucks on net, and it suits Schaefer in particular. Winnipeg's goaltending sits 23rd in GSAx, so volume should turn into goals.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs. weak kills
keyMatchups.body: Winnipeg (72.1%) and Detroit (71.4%) both kill penalties in the bottom third of the league. If the 28th-ranked Islanders power play can't produce here, the problem is structural rather than bad luck.

keyMatchups.title: Toronto's power play vs. NYI kill
keyMatchups.body: Toronto converts 26.7% on the power play, sixth best, against an Islanders kill ranked fourth. The Leafs also rank 24th at holding down wingers, which favors Holmstrom and Eklund. Toronto's -4.3 Pts vs Goal Diff suggests a team that has lost close games rather than one that is outclassed.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Islanders can out-shoot weak opponents like Columbus and Toronto, or keep needing Sorokin to steal games they should control.

restOfSeason.body:
The goaltending is the sustainable part. Two of the last four seasons ended around 40 goals saved above expected, and Sorokin's track record supports a top-ten group even if this pace eases. The 12.2% team shooting and the 103.2 all-situations PDO are the parts that will drift back. With a below-average shot share and a power play near the bottom, that pulls the goal differential toward even. The kill should stay strong, and the even overtime luck means the points total is not inflated.

The likely result is a team that gives back a little of its 95-point pace and lands around the wild-card line. In this division that means fighting the Rangers and Washington rather than chasing Carolina. A meaningful jump would require the power play to reach league average or the blueline behind Schaefer to stop bleeding chances.
swingFactors: Power-play conversion climbing toward league average

confidence.note: 19 games is a small sample; shooting and PDO will move, but the goalie-driven profile matches recent seasons.
